summary: Describes the mechanisms that allow a JavaScript application to control the signaling plane of a multimedia session through the W3C RTCPeerConnection API, and how this relates to existing signaling protocols. It was replaced by RFC 9429.

eli5.summary: A web page gets the controls to set up a call without knowing every detail of how.

questions: how does javascript control webrtc signaling
subtitle: How a JavaScript app controls WebRTC multimedia session setup without understanding the signaling details.

tldr.problem: WebRTC applications need to set up multimedia sessions (audio, video, data) but should not have to understand complex signaling protocols. Different applications prefer different signaling (SIP, XMPP, proprietary systems), so a standard way to decouple signaling from the media engine is needed.
tldr.mechanism: JSEP (JavaScript Session Establishment Protocol) separates the signaling logic from the media engine. The JavaScript application controls the signaling protocol and message exchange entirely; JSEP provides simple APIs to create session descriptions (offers and answers in SDP format), apply them to the media engine, and manage ICE candidates for connectivity. The application handles all signaling transport and protocol details.
tldr.outcome: JSEP became replaced by RFC 9429 with updates. It is the foundation of WebRTC, enabling web applications to establish video calls, screen sharing, and data transfer with flexible signaling.

facts.label: Serialization
facts.value: Text-based with 'a=', 'm=', and other SDP attributes

facts.label: Core API calls
facts.value: createOffer, createAnswer, setLocalDescription, setRemoteDescription, addTrack, addIceCandidate

facts.label: Encryption
facts.value: DTLS for media, specified in SDP via DTLS fingerprints

today: RFC 9429 is the current JSEP specification, with clarifications and updates. JSEP is the foundation of WebRTC, used in web browsers, Electron apps, and mobile WebRTC implementations for video conferencing, screen sharing, and real-time data transfer.

sections.title: Decoupling Signaling from Media
sections.content:
WebRTC (Web Real-Time Communication) lets web browsers establish multimedia sessions directly with each other. However, the browser needs to know what codecs the other side supports, which ports to use, how to encrypt the connection, and other details before media can flow. This information is traditionally exchanged via a signaling protocol like SIP or XMPP. JSEP separates this concern: the JavaScript application (running in the browser) controls the signaling protocol entirely, while the browser's media engine controls only the media plane.

This design allows web developers to use any signaling protocol they prefer. A library can implement SIP on top of JSEP, or a site can use WebSockets to send JSON messages, or a custom protocol. JSEP simply provides the APIs to generate and consume session descriptions in SDP (Session Description Protocol) format, which describe what media can be exchanged and how.

The key insight is that JSEP gathers no application-level knowledge of the signaling. It does not know about call glare, retransmission, forking, or other signaling-layer concepts. These are entirely the JavaScript application's responsibility. The application is responsible for implementing the state machine of its chosen signaling protocol and converting session descriptions and ICE candidates into its protocol's messages.
sections.eli5: The browser's media engine is like a translator who only speaks about codecs and ports. The JavaScript application is the conductor who decides to use Spanish or French to call the other person. JSEP connects the two: the conductor tells the translator 'Here is what the other person said' and asks 'What can we send?'

sections.title: Session Descriptions and State Machine
sections.content:
The core of JSEP is the exchange of session descriptions using the offer/answer model from RFC 3264. When initiating a session, the application calls createOffer to generate a session description that specifies what media types and codecs the local side supports, what ICE candidates it can use, and other capabilities. The application then calls setLocalDescription to apply this offer to the media engine, and sends the offer to the remote side via its signaling mechanism.

The remote side, upon receiving the offer, calls setRemoteDescription to apply it to its media engine, then calls createAnswer to generate a complementary answer describing what media types it will actually use (a subset of what was offered, negotiated to the intersection of capabilities). It applies this answer with setLocalDescription and sends it back.

When the initiator receives the answer, it calls setRemoteDescription, and at that point both sides have a complete picture of what media will be exchanged. The JSEP state machine ensures that offers and answers are applied in the correct order: offers are 'pending' until an answer is applied, and multiple provisional answers can be applied (useful for sequential call forking where multiple callees respond) before a final answer commits the session configuration.
sections.eli5: Alice says 'I can send video and audio' (createOffer). Bob receives this and says 'I accept video, but only audio if it is Opus codec' (createAnswer). They exchange these descriptions, apply them, and now they both know exactly what to send to each other.

sections.title: Media Control: Transceivers, Senders, and Receivers
sections.content:
The JavaScript application controls media using RtpTransceivers (objects that represent bidirectional RTP media for one media type). Each transceiver has an RtpSender (controls outgoing media) and an RtpReceiver (represents incoming media). The application can call addTrack to add a local media track to send, createDataChannel to create a data channel, or addTransceiver to pre-allocate a transceiver for media it will send or receive.

When the application calls createOffer or createAnswer, the JSEP implementation generates an SDP 'm=' section for each transceiver. The order and count of transceivers must match between local and remote descriptions, though for initial offers the application can create any number of 'm=' sections. Once an offer is applied, the remote side's answer must contain the same number of 'm=' sections, in the same order.

The application can control what each transceiver does: sendrecv (send and receive media), sendonly (send media only), recvonly (receive media only), or inactive (no media). This flexibility supports various call scenarios including hold (sendrecv to inactive), mute (sendrecv to recvonly), and call on hold from the remote side.
sections.eli5: Each 'm=' section is a transceiver: a two-way audio or video channel. You can add tracks to send, add transceivers to prepare to receive, and tell each one whether to send, receive, both, or neither.

sections.title: ICE Candidates and Connection Establishment
sections.content:
While session descriptions tell both sides what media to exchange, they do not directly specify how to reach each other over the network. JSEP decouples this by separating ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) from the signaling state machine. ICE works separately to find the best network path between the two peers.

When the media engine needs ICE candidates (because a new 'm=' section was added or an ICE restart is needed), it enters a 'gathering phase' and notifies the application via an onicecandidate event. The application receives candidates one at a time as they are gathered. It can send these immediately to the remote side (Trickle ICE) allowing media setup to start before all candidates are gathered, or wait until gathering completes and send them all at once with the session description.

Once gathering is complete, the JSEP implementation fires an onicecandidate event with a null candidate to signal the end of gathering. The application can use this to know when to send the complete offer/answer with all candidates.

JSEP also supports ICE candidate policies: an application can request that only relay candidates (those through a TURN server) be used for privacy, or allow all candidates for performance. This filtering is applied at the JSEP implementation level, so the application never sees candidates it is not allowed to use.
sections.eli5: The media engine sends you a list of 'Here is a way to reach me: 192.0.2.1:50000' or 'Or try 203.0.113.5:10000 through a relay server.' You send this list to the other person. When they send you their list, you feed it to the media engine and it picks the best path.

sections.title: Simulcast and Forking
sections.content:
JSEP supports advanced features like simulcast (sending multiple encodings of the same video at different bitrates) and forking (handling multiple simultaneous calls from a single offer). For simulcast, the application configures multiple encodings on an RtpSender; JSEP generates SDP with simulcast markings, and if the remote side accepts, the media engine will send all configured encodings on a single 'm=' section, allowing a server to choose which encoding to send to each viewer.

For sequential forking (one offer sent to multiple recipients, with only one accepting), JSEP supports provisional answers: the application can apply multiple answers as 'pranswer' (provisional answer) and apply only one as a final 'answer'. This allows, for example, the first responding callee to be connected while rejecting later responses, or the last responding callee to be connected by reapplying the provisional answer as final.

For parallel forking (exchanging media with multiple peers simultaneously), the application simply creates multiple PeerConnection objects, each with the same local tracks, generating multiple independent offers for multiple peers.
sections.eli5: Simulcast is sending the same video at three different qualities at once so the other side (usually a server) can pick which one to forward to each viewer. For forking, you can say 'maybe' to multiple callers and then later say 'yes' to the best one.

messages.label: setRemoteDescription(answer)
messages.note: Apply remote answer; media setup complete.
